title: Ofe Akwu
localName: Ofe akwu — Igbo palm nut soup
author: Jemimah Ogunleye
desc: The Igbo banga — same palm nut base, but with scent leaf and ugu added, and served over boiled rice rather than with a swallow.
longDesc: Ofe akwu is the Igbo version of banga and the two differences are exactly what the author names: the leaves and the accompaniment. A quarter cup of scent leaf and half a cup of ugu go in near the end, which the Delta version deliberately leaves out, and the whole thing is eaten with boiled white rice rather than with starch or a swallow. The technique detail worth having is that the fresh fish is cooked five or six minutes, lifted out so it does not break up, and returned for the last two minutes.
ingredients: Small chunk ogiri okpei or dawadawa
steps: Season and boil the meats until tender, adding the stockfish as they go.
Blend the scotch bonnets and the ogiri okpei or dawadawa with a little water, add to the pot, and simmer 2 minutes.
Combine the palm nut extract with the meat stock on low heat and adjust the seasoning.
Add the fresh fish and cook 5 to 6 minutes, then remove it to prevent it breaking.
Return the cooked meats with the crayfish and cook 5 minutes.
Return the fish and cook 2 minutes.
Take it off the heat and let it stand 2 to 3 minutes, so the oil settles on the surface.
chefTips: Scent leaf and ugu are what make it Igbo rather than Delta. The author states the distinction outright and it is the cleanest regional marker in the banga family.
Lift the fish out after its first five or six minutes and put it back at the end. It is the only way to serve it whole.
Boiled white rice, not a swallow. Ofe akwu over rice is the standard pairing in the southeast.
Let it stand two or three minutes off the heat so the oil settles on top. That glossy orange surface is what a finished ofe akwu looks like.
A 400 g tin is the practical route. For the from-scratch palm nut cream see NGA043.
No oburunbebe stick here, and no banga spice blend. That is the other difference from the Delta versions — the Igbo soup leans on ogiri and scent leaf instead.
Ogiri okpei or dawadawa, a small chunk, blended with the peppers. It dissolves completely and you will not see it in the finished soup.
commonMistakes: Leaving the fresh fish in for the whole cook.
Omitting the scent leaf, which makes it a Delta banga.
Serving it with a swallow rather than rice.
Stirring after the fish goes back in.
Adding banga spice, which belongs to the Delta version.
sources: Adapted from 'Ofe Akwu', byline Sisi Jemimah. Quantities as printed: 600g assorted meats; 1 medium fresh fish; 2-3 stockfish pieces; 1 tin (400g) palm nut extract; 1/4 cup scent leaves/basil/Efinrin; 1/2 cup ugu leaves; 2 tablespoons ground crayfish; 2 Knorr chicken cubes; chicken/beef seasoning; small chunk ogiri okpei or dawadawa; 3-4 scotch bonnet; salt.

THE REGIONAL DISTINCTION, as printed: 'It is the Igbo version of the all-too-popular Banga soup', and — unlike the Delta variant served with starch or swallows — 'the Igbo preparation is typically paired with boiled rice.' Her Delta banga page states the other half of the distinction: 'The Igbo version is called Ofe Akwu which includes the addition of Ugu or Scent leaves which is without in the Delta version' (NGA045).

Times as printed: blended peppers and ogiri simmer 2 minutes; fresh fish 5 to 6 minutes then removed 'to prevent breaking'; cooked meats and crayfish 5 minutes; scent leaves; fish returned 2 minutes; ugu; heat off, residual 2 to 3 minutes 'to let the oil settle on the surface'. Yield not specified.

CROSS-REGIONAL NAMING, from the Kitchen Butterfly banga page: the same dish is Obe Eyin in Yoruba, Ofe Akwu in Igbo, Banga in Edo, Delta and Urhobo, Obe-Ekpo in Itsekiri, Lii Fulou or Luu Fiai in Bayelsa, and Efere Abak or Atama in Akwa Ibom and Cross River. Across West Africa: Sauce Graine in Togo and Benin, Mbanga in Cameroon, Abe nkwan in Ghana.

Nigerian Food TV makes the same comparison from the Delta side, stating that banga 'is very similar to the Igbo's Ofe Akwu' but that the 'additional spices used for preparing Banga Soup, makes it differ in taste and aroma', naming the oburunbebe stick and the banga spices as the essential differentiators.
The Itsekiri National Congress adds a third claimed difference — extraction method, cold against hot — and contrasts banga with ofe akwu on that basis (NGA046).
reheating: Gentle heat. Add the greens fresh if you can.
healthBenefits: Palm nut pulp is rich in carotenoids and tocotrienols.
Scent leaf carries aromatic oils with antimicrobial activity.
Ugu supplies iron, calcium and fibre.
Very low in carbohydrate before the rice.
culturalNote: That one soup is called banga in the Delta, ofe akwu in Igboland and obe eyin in Yorubaland — and that each community argues for its own spices, leaves and accompaniment — makes the palm nut soup family a good map of southern Nigeria. The ingredients barely change. What changes is the aromatics and what you eat it with, and those are the things people are most attached to.
